lead: A network function is a ratio of one response transform to one excitation transform. Kill every independent source, set all initial energy to zero, and the circuit becomes a pure ratio H(s). That single function carries the poles that decide the natural response and the zeros that shape how the steady-state response rises or falls. Designers use it to read stability from a pole-zero plot, to get the impulse response by inverse transform, and to find the sinusoidal steady-state gain as H(jω). Filters, amplifiers and control loops are all specified this way.
prereq: You need: Laplace analysis for s-domain algebra, and series resonance and Q from resonance and coupled circuits.

blocks.text: Write the circuit in the s-domain with the Laplace transform. Element impedances become: R stays R, L becomes sL, C becomes 1/(sC). Set every independent source to zero: voltage sources become short circuits, current sources become open circuits. Set every initial inductor current and initial capacitor voltage to zero. Now excite one port with a test source X(s) and compute the response Y(s) at the chosen port.

The network function is H(s) = Y(s)/X(s). X(s) is the input transform; Y(s) is the output transform; H(s) has units of output per input. If input and output are at the same port, H is a driving-point function, such as input impedance Z(s) = V(s)/I(s). If they are at different ports, H is a transfer function, such as voltage gain V₂(s)/V₁(s).

blocks.where: N(s) and D(s) are polynomials in s with real coefficients; N(s) is the numerator, D(s) is the denominator after cancelling common factors.

blocks.text: The denominator D(s) is the characteristic polynomial of the circuit. Its roots are the poles: they are the natural frequencies of the circuit with its sources killed, so many network functions of one circuit share them. The roots of the numerator N(s) are the zeros, and they depend on both where the input is applied and where the output is taken.

items: Draw the s-domain circuit with all independent sources killed and zero initial conditions.
Apply a test source X(s) at the input port.
Solve for the response Y(s) at the output port.
Form H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), then factor N(s) and D(s).

blocks.text: A pole is a value of s that makes H(s) infinite. A zero is a value of s that makes H(s) zero. Write s = σ + jω. σ is the real part, in s⁻¹; ω is the imaginary part, in rad/s; j is the imaginary unit. Mark poles by × and zeros by ○ in the complex s-plane. The real part σ sets growth or decay; the imaginary part ω sets oscillation.
H(s) = K (s − z₁)(s − z₂)… / ((s − p₁)(s − p₂)…)
blocks.where: K is a real gain; z₁, z₂, … are zeros; p₁, p₂, … are poles. A repeated pole or zero is counted by its multiplicity.

blocks.text: With zero initial conditions, the impulse response is h(t) = L⁻¹{H(s)}. Each simple pole pᵢ contributes a term Aᵢ e<sup>pᵢt</sup>. A pole with negative real part gives a decaying term. A pole on the jω axis gives a constant-amplitude sinusoid. A pole with positive real part gives growth. So stability needs all poles strictly in the left half plane.

Put s = jω to get the sinusoidal steady-state ratio. |H(jω)| is the gain at frequency ω, and ∠H(jω) is the phase shift. If a pole sits close to the jω axis, the denominator becomes small near that frequency and |H(jω)| peaks. This is the resonance peak of a high-Q circuit: small damping means a tall, narrow peak.

blocks.where: N(jω) and D(jω) are the numerator and denominator evaluated at s = jω; | | means magnitude, and ω is in rad/s.

sections.h3: Stability and reading a pole-zero plot

blocks.text: Only poles decide stability. Zeros change the size and phase of the response but cannot turn a growing exponential into a decaying one. A simple pole at s = 0 puts a constant, non-decaying term in the impulse response, so the step response ramps without limit; a pair at s = ±jω₀ is a sustained oscillation; a pole at s = +2 gives e<sup>2t</sup>. Only a zero exactly on a pole removes that pole's term. A zero that is merely near it leaves a small residue, and a slow pole still sets the long tail of the response.

For a second-order low-pass H(s) = ω<sub>n</sub>² / (s² + 2ζω<sub>n</sub> s + ω<sub>n</sub>²), poles are s = −ζω<sub>n</sub> ± jω_n√(1 − ζ²) for 0 < ζ < 1. The damping ratio ζ sets the real part; the natural frequency ω<sub>n</sub> sets the distance from the origin. For ζ < 1/√2 the magnitude has a peak at ω<sub>r</sub> = ω<sub>n</sub>√(1 − 2ζ²) with peak 1/[2ζ√(1 − ζ²)].

figure.caption: The worked example. Left: the poles of H(s) = 100/(s² + (R/L)s + 100) sit on a circle of radius ωₙ = 10 rad/s, close to the jω axis for R = 2 Ω and further left for R = 10 Ω. Right: the pole near the axis gives the tall peak of 5.03 near 9.9 rad/s; the R = 10 Ω curve peaks at only 1.15.

spec.aria: Left: s-plane with poles at minus 1 plus or minus j9.95 and at minus 5 plus or minus j8.66 on a dashed circle of radius 10. Right: magnitude of H against omega from 0 to 20 rad per second, with a peak of 5.03 near 9.9 for R 2 ohms and a peak of 1.15 near 7.07 for R 10 ohms.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has L = 1 H, C = 0.01 F, and the output is the capacitor voltage. The input is an ideal voltage source. Find H(s) = V<sub>C</sub>(s)/V<sub>s</sub>(s), its poles and zeros, and the peak magnitude for R = 2 Ω and R = 10 Ω. Use ω<sub>n</sub> and ζ.
steps: For a series RLC with output across C, voltage division in the s-domain gives H(s) = (1/(sC)) / (R + sL + 1/(sC)). Multiply numerator and denominator by sC: H(s) = 1 / (LC s² + RC s + 1). With L = 1 H and C = 0.01 F, LC = 0.01 s². Divide by 0.01: H(s) = 100 / (s² + (R/L)s + 100). With L = 1 H the middle coefficient R/L, in s⁻¹, has the same number as R in ohms, so it reads s² + Rs + 100.

The natural frequency is ω<sub>n</sub> = √(1/(LC)) = √(100) = 10 rad/s. The denominator is s² + 2ζω<sub>n</sub> s + ω<sub>n</sub>², so 2ζω<sub>n</sub> = R/L, giving ζ = R/(2ω<sub>n</sub>) = R/20. For R = 2 Ω, ζ = 0.1. For R = 10 Ω, ζ = 0.5.
The numerator is the constant 100, so there are no finite zeros.
examples.answer: H(s) = 100/(s² + (R/L)s + 100) with no finite zeros; for R = 2 Ω the poles are −1 ± j9.9499 and peak |H| = 5.0252; for R = 10 Ω the poles are −5 ± j8.6603 and peak |H| = 1.1547, with |H| = 1 at ω = 10 rad/s.
examples.check:
import math
wn = math.sqrt(1/(1*0.01))
print(round(wn**2, 4))
for R in (2, 10):
    zeta = R/(2*wn)
    print(round(zeta, 4))
    re = -zeta*wn
    im = wn*math.sqrt(1-zeta**2)
    print(round(re, 4))
    print(round(im, 4))
    wr = wn*math.sqrt(1-2*zeta**2)
    print(round(wr, 4))
    peak = 1/(2*zeta*math.sqrt(1-zeta**2))
    print(round(peak, 4))
print(round(100/math.sqrt((100-100)**2+(10*10)**2), 4))

traps: Stability comes only from poles. A zero in the right half plane does not make an unstable circuit; a pole in the right half plane does.
A pole on the jω axis is marginal, not stable. It gives sustained oscillation; any small positive real part grows without limit.
Do not forget to kill sources and zero initial conditions before forming H(s). A live source or an initial capacitor voltage adds terms that are not part of H(s).
H(jω) is not H(s) with s replaced by ω. Put s = jω, including the j. Dropping j gives the wrong sign and phase.
Cancelling a pole with a zero hides it mathematically only; exact cancellation is not robust in real components.

quiz.a: A network function is H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), the ratio of the Laplace transform of a chosen response Y(s) to the Laplace transform of a chosen excitation X(s), with all independent sources killed and all initial conditions zero.

quiz.q: Why do we kill independent sources and set initial conditions to zero when finding H(s)?
quiz.a: H(s) must describe only the circuit's own input-output relation. A live source adds a forced term, and initial energy adds a natural term. Removing both leaves the pure ratio that depends only on the network elements and the chosen ports.

quiz.q: For H(s) = 25/(s² + 4s + 25), find ω<sub>n</sub>, ζ and the poles.
quiz.a: ω<sub>n</sub>² = 25, so ω<sub>n</sub> = 5 rad/s. 2ζω<sub>n</sub> = 4, so ζ = 4/(10) = 0.4. Poles solve s² + 4s + 25 = 0: s = −2 ± j√21 = −2 ± j4.5826.

quiz.q: A circuit has poles at −2 and +1. Is it stable? What time-domain term does each pole give?
quiz.a: It is unstable because one pole is in the right half plane. The pole at −2 gives a decaying term e<sup>−2t</sup>. The pole at +1 gives a growing term e<sup>t</sup>.

quiz.q: A 2 Ω resistor in series with a 1 H inductor is connected in parallel with a 0.5 F capacitor. Find the driving-point impedance Z(s), its poles and zeros, and check Z(0).
quiz.a: Z(s) = (s + 2)(2/s) / (s + 2 + 2/s) = 2(s + 2)/(s² + 2s + 2). Zero at s = −2; poles at s = −1 ± j1. Check: Z(0) = 4/2 = 2 Ω, the DC value with L a short and C open.

quiz.q: Two circuits have the same poles but different zeros. Compare their natural responses and their sinusoidal steady-state magnitudes.
quiz.a: The natural responses have the same exponential decay and same oscillation because the poles are the same. The magnitudes |H(jω)| and phases can differ because the zeros change the numerator N(jω). Stability is still decided by the shared poles alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, pole-zero maps are read in control and filter design before any simulation: left-half-plane distance sets settling, and jω-axis proximity sets peaking. Network analysers measure S-parameters, and from these tools extract poles and zeros for RF filters and high-speed links. Search next for Bode plot, root locus, second-order low-pass filter, and stability of linear systems.
